claim: Pickering-2 (1983) channel G16: a displaced garter spring let the hot pressure tube touch the cool calandria tube; hydrogen moved to the cold spot, formed brittle hydride blisters, and delayed hydride cracking followed
source_quote: in 1983 a Zircaloy-2 pressure tube in channel G16 failed unstably at full power in Pickering Unit 2 ... The outlet end spacer had moved towards the centre of the channel allowing the pressure tube to sag by creep and touch the calandria tube towards the outlet end. The thermal gradients set up in the pressure tube from contact caused hydrogen to migrate to the coldest point and precipitate as solid hydride accretions, commonly called blisters. ... The crack grew by the delayed hydride cracking mechanism.
note: AECL fuel channel report 108US-31100-LS-001 (2003) on NRC ADAMS; supports the dew analogy (hydrogen to the coldest point). Also 'August 1983' (p.11).
